notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
The working vocabulary of Model Evaluation — learn these cold; everything else in the module hangs off them.
- **Choosing the metric that matches the business cost** — Match it to the business cost of each mistake type — the metric is a contract with the stakeholder, not a default.
- **Confusion matrices read properly** — The off-diagonal cells are the story — they show exactly how the model fails.

modules.title: RE-Bench: Agents Doing ML Research
modules.summary: Welcome to the benchmark that grades AI on your own craft. I'm your instructor for this module, and we're studying RE-Bench — METR's head-to-head contest between AI agents and human experts at real machine-learning research engineering: fitting scaling laws, optimizing GPU kernels, designing architectures under constraints. You'll learn how the benchmark is built, what the 2h/8h/32h crossover tells us about where agents help and where they don't, and how to read any 'AI does research' claim with an evaluator's eye. All figures as of October 7, 2026.
objectives: Describe RE-Bench's design: contamination-free environments, calibrated 0–1 scoring, faithful human baselines
Explain the 2h/8h/32h crossover and what it implies for human–agent collaboration in ML research
Apply the critical-reading checklist to 'AI does ML research' claims

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **RE-Bench** — METR's benchmark (2024-11-22) for AI-led ML research engineering: 7 realistic, open-ended environments, agents vs human experts, same resources and time limits.
- **Anti-contamination design** — Environments built from scratch; most held back unpublished. Public tasks can't separate capability from memorization.
- **Calibrated scoring** — 0 = starting solution's score, 1 = METR's strong reference solution; comparable across environments.
- **Human baselines** — 71 attempts by 61 experts, up to 8 hours each; 82% non-zero, 24% matched or beat the reference.
- **The 2h/8h/32h crossover** — Agents ~4× humans at 2h; humans narrowly lead at 8h; humans ~2× the top agent at 32h across attempts.
- **The kernel example** — o1-preview's custom CUDA kernel: 0.64 ms vs best human 0.67 ms (start 4.74 ms, reference 1.60 ms) — a data point, not a verdict.
- **Capability of concern** — AI automation of AI R&D is the monitored capability; RE-Bench is the reusable instrument.

notes.title: Worked estimation
notes.body:
Score an RE-Bench-style ML task yourself.
1. **Pick a research-engineering task** with a measurable objective — e.g., fit a scaling law from provided training runs, or optimize a small kernel.
2. **Define the scoring function** and calibrate it: 0 = the baseline you're given, 1 = a strong reference solution you write (or borrow and verify).
3. **Set the time budget** and run both sides: an agent with a fixed attempt budget, and yourself (or a colleague) with the same clock.
4. **Score best-of-k** across attempts at 2h, then extend to 8h. Watch for the crossover pattern: where does the agent's 10×+ iteration speed win, and where does coherent long-horizon work take over?
5. **Write the limitations** before the conclusions: one task, one agent, one human — what would you need to make this a claim about 'AI doing research'?

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Replicate one RE-Bench-style environment from scratch. Do not adapt a public tutorial — build the task, the starting code, and the scoring function yourself. Deliverable: the environment plus a 1-page report with (1) the task and why it's realistic ML research engineering, (2) your calibrated 0 and 1, (3) a timed human attempt (yours or a colleague's) and an agent attempt under the same budget, (4) the comparison, and (5) a limitations section. Grading bar: the limitations section must name contamination risk, baseline quality, and feedback-loop realism — the three things that separate an eval from a demo.

What endures: the design pattern — contamination-free tasks, calibrated scoring, real human baselines, reported budgets. Cite the date; report the budgets.

from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

                 ('clf', LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])

print(f'honest score: {fixed:.4f}')
print(f'inflation   : {leaky - fixed:+.4f}')
print('Audit rule: every transformation that learns from data '
      'must live inside the pipeline, fit on train only.')

scriptLabs.solution:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 1))
y = 3 * X[:, 0] + 1 + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=200)
Xb = np.c_[np.ones(200), X]

def gradient_descent(Xb, y, lr, steps):
    n = len(y)
    theta = np.zeros(Xb.shape[1])
    for _ in range(steps):
        grad = (2.0 / n) * Xb.T @ (Xb @ theta - y)
        theta = theta - lr * grad
    return theta

print('lr=0.1 :', gradient_descent(Xb, y, lr=0.1, steps=500))   # ~[1, 3]
print('lr=1.5 :', gradient_descent(Xb, y, lr=1.5, steps=500))   # diverges -> inf/nan
print('Closed form check:', np.linalg.lstsq(Xb, y, rcond=None)[0])

import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

docs = [
    'Gradient descent updates parameters against the gradient of the loss.',
    'Bagging averages many models to reduce variance.',
    'Precision is TP / (TP + FP); recall is TP / (TP + FN).',
    'LoRA adapts large models by training low-rank update matrices.',
]
questions = [
    ('how do you lower variance with ensembles', 1),
    ('what is the precision formula', 2),
]
vec = TfidfVectorizer().fit(docs)
D = vec.transform(docs)
hits = 0
for text, gold in questions:
    q = vec.transform([text])
    scores = cosine_similarity(q, D)[0]
    ranked = np.argsort(-scores)
    print(f'Q: {text}')
    for r in ranked[:2]:
        print(f'  [{r}] ({scores[r]:.3f}) {docs[r]}')
    hits += int(gold in ranked[:2])
recall_at_2 = hits / len(questions)
print(f'recall@2 = {recall_at_2:.2f}')

drills.title: Baseline first
drills.prompt: Why does the applied ML loop insist on a simple baseline before any tuning?
choices: It sets the bar later models must clear, so complexity has to earn its keep
It replaces the need for evaluation
drills.explain: Without a baseline you cannot tell whether a fancy model is actually better than the obvious thing.

drills.title: Leakage
drills.prompt: Which of these is target leakage?
choices: Scaling features inside a pipeline fit on train
Computing the target mean per category on the full dataset before splitting
drills.explain: Statistics computed from the full dataset — including the target — leak future information into training.

drills.title: Metric choice
drills.prompt: Fraud detection: 0.1% positives, missing fraud costs 100x a false alarm. Best primary metric?
choices: Precision at a fixed recall, or cost-weighted loss
drills.explain: Accuracy is dominated by the majority class; the metric must encode the asymmetric business cost.

drills.title: Calibration
drills.prompt: A model is well calibrated when…
choices: Its predicted probabilities match observed frequencies
It never predicts the minority class
drills.explain: Calibration means a predicted 0.7 happens about 70% of the time — probabilities that mean something.

drills.title: Bagging
drills.explain: Averaging models trained on different bootstrap samples cancels uncorrelated error: variance drops, bias is roughly unchanged.

drills.title: Boosting
drills.prompt: Gradient boosting fits each new tree to…
choices: The residuals (remaining errors) of the ensemble so far
drills.explain: Boosting is sequential error correction: each weak learner targets what the ensemble still gets wrong.

drills.title: Adam vs SGD
drills.prompt: Adam’s main practical advantage over plain SGD is…
choices: Per-parameter adaptive learning rates, less manual schedule tuning
It only works on convex problems
drills.explain: Adam adapts the step size per parameter from gradient moment estimates — convenient, though tuned SGD can generalize better.

drills.title: SHAP
choices: Per-prediction feature attributions grounded in game theory
drills.explain: SHAP attributes each prediction to features via Shapley values — local explanations with a principled foundation.

drills.title: Self-attention
drills.prompt: In self-attention, each token’s representation is…
choices: A weighted mix of all tokens’ values, weights from query-key similarity
Computed only from the previous token
drills.explain: Attention lets every position gather context: weights = softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d)), output = weights · V.

drills.title: LoRA
choices: Training low-rank update matrices while the base weights stay frozen
drills.explain: LoRA learns BA-style low-rank deltas added to frozen weights — a fraction of the trainable parameters.

drills.title: RAG failure
drills.prompt: A RAG system answers confidently but the retrieved chunks are irrelevant. First fix to try?
choices: Improve retrieval: chunking, hybrid search, reranking
drills.explain: If retrieval is wrong, the generator has nothing good to ground on — fix the retriever before touching generation.

drills.title: Eval harness
drills.prompt: The single most valuable artifact for shipping LLM features safely is…
choices: A golden dataset with regression evals run on every change
drills.explain: Golden cases plus automated regression checks turn “hope it still works” into a verifiable gate.

scenarios.title: Model selection under constraints
scenarios.context: You must pick a model for a tabular churn problem: 50k rows, nightly batch scoring, the team knows scikit-learn, and the business wants an explanation for each flagged account.

steps.prompt: Which family do you start with?

options.text: Gradient-boosted trees with a logistic-regression baseline first
options.why: Trees dominate tabular data at this scale, and the baseline tells you whether the complexity earns its keep — plus both are explainable via SHAP/feature importance.

options.text: A deep MLP, because deep learning is state of the art
options.why: On 50k tabular rows, MLPs rarely beat boosted trees and are harder to explain — the module is explicit that trees usually win here.

options.text: An LLM prompted with each row
options.why: Per-row LLM calls are expensive, slow, and unexplainable for batch scoring — wrong tool for structured tabular data.

steps.prompt: Stakeholders ask why account #1042 was flagged. Your move?

options.text: Show SHAP values for that prediction plus the model’s global feature importance
options.why: Local attributions answer ‘why this account’; global importance shows the pattern. Both are covered in the interpretation module.

options.text: Say the model is a black box that cannot be explained
options.why: Tree models are among the most explainable — claiming otherwise forfeits stakeholder trust unnecessarily.

options.text: Retrain without that account and compare
options.why: Leave-one-out retraining answers a different question (influence), not ‘which features drove this prediction’.

steps.prompt: The model’s predicted churn probabilities feed a budget decision. What must hold?

options.text: Nothing — ranking is enough
options.why: Budget decisions multiply probability by value; uncalibrated scores make the expected-value math wrong.

options.text: The probabilities must be calibrated, checked on a held-out set
options.why: When probabilities drive money decisions, calibration — predicted 0.3 happening ~30% of the time — is the requirement, verified out-of-sample.

options.text: The model must reach 99% accuracy
options.why: Accuracy is the wrong bar on imbalanced churn data and says nothing about probability quality.

scenarios.title: Build vs retrieve: the GenAI call
scenarios.context: Support wants an assistant that answers from 2,000 internal docs. You have a small team, no GPU cluster, and a tight budget.

steps.prompt: Fine-tune a 70B model or build RAG?

options.text: RAG: retrieve passages, generate with citations
options.why: With 2,000 docs and no GPU cluster, RAG grounds answers in current sources, is cheaper, and citations make answers auditable — fine-tuning bakes in knowledge that goes stale.

options.text: Fine-tune the 70B model on all docs
options.why: Fine-tuning memorizes unstably, costs far more, and cannot cite sources — the wrong choice for a doc-QA task on a budget.

options.text: Prompt the base model with no retrieval
options.why: Without grounding, the model will hallucinate confident answers about internal docs it never saw.

steps.prompt: Users complain the assistant cites irrelevant passages. Diagnosis?

options.text: The generator’s temperature is too high
options.why: Temperature affects sampling randomness, not which passages were retrieved — this is a retrieval problem.

options.text: Retrieval quality: fix chunking, add hybrid search and reranking, measure recall@k
options.why: Irrelevant citations mean the retriever failed. Chunking, hybrid lexical+dense search, and reranking are the documented fixes, verified with recall@k.

options.text: Switch to a larger embedding model blindly
options.why: Bigger embeddings without measurement is guessing — evaluate on your task first, per the embeddings module.

steps.prompt: Before launch, what proves the system is safe to ship?

options.text: A good demo to the team
options.why: Demos show the happy path. Shipping needs evidence: golden cases, regression evals, and a failure catalog.

options.text: A golden eval set, regression runs on every change, and a documented failure catalog
options.why: The eval-harness module’s rule: golden datasets, automated regression checks, and an honest catalog of where the system still fails.

options.text: Benchmark scores from the model vendor
options.why: Vendor benchmarks measure the base model on public tasks — not your RAG system on your docs.

scenarios.title: The too-good model
scenarios.context: A teammate reports 0.99 AUC on a fraud model. The business is thrilled. You are suspicious.

options.text: Celebrate and ship it
options.why: A 0.99 on fraud is a leakage smell until proven otherwise — shipping it risks a production embarrassment.

options.text: Audit for leakage: when each feature becomes available relative to the label, and whether preprocessing saw the test set
options.why: The leakage-audit checklist: features must respect causality (no future info), and all learned transformations belong inside a train-only pipeline.

options.text: Tune hyperparameters to push it to 0.995
options.why: Tuning a leaky pipeline optimizes a fiction — fix the evaluation first.

steps.prompt: You find a feature computed from post-label events. What now?

options.text: Keep it — it helps accuracy
options.why: That feature will not exist at prediction time in production. The model is learning the future.

options.text: Remove it or rebuild it using only information available at prediction time, then re-evaluate honestly
options.why: Datetime features must respect causality. Rebuild with as-of-prediction-time data and report the honest number.

options.text: Hide it from the report
options.why: Hiding leakage is dishonest and the production model will still fail.

mockTasks.q: The applied ML loop, in order, is:
choices: Frame, data, baseline, evaluate, iterate, ship
mockTasks.explain: Frame the problem, get the data, build a baseline, evaluate, iterate, and only then ship.

mockTasks.q: Preprocessing must live inside the pipeline because:
choices: It keeps transformations fit on train only, preventing leakage and aiding reproducibility
mockTasks.explain: Pipelines guarantee every learned transformation is fit inside each fold/split — leakage dies, reproducibility is born.

mockTasks.q: On imbalanced data, accuracy is misleading because:
choices: A majority-class classifier scores high while learning nothing
mockTasks.explain: Predicting the majority class can yield 99% accuracy on 1% positives — use precision/recall or cost-weighted metrics.

mockTasks.q: Random forests are a strong default mainly because:
choices: Bagging plus random feature subsets cut variance with little tuning
mockTasks.explain: Averaging deep, decorrelated trees reduces variance while staying robust — the practitioner’s strong default.

mockTasks.q: Bayes’ rule as an updating discipline means:
choices: Updating beliefs from prior to posterior as evidence arrives
mockTasks.explain: Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior: a principled way to fold new evidence into existing beliefs.

mockTasks.q: Entity embeddings help with high-cardinality categoricals by:
choices: Learning dense vectors that capture similarity between categories
mockTasks.explain: Embeddings map categories like zip codes into a space where similar categories sit near each other — learnable by the network.

choices: Starting small to avoid early instability, then ramping up
mockTasks.explain: Large initial steps on uncalibrated weights cause divergence; warmup ramps the rate safely.

choices: How the predicted output varies with one feature, marginalizing others
mockTasks.explain: PDPs visualize the marginal effect of a feature on predictions — global interpretation.

choices: Operate on mismatched shapes by implicit expansion, avoiding explicit loops
mockTasks.explain: Broadcasting vectorizes operations across shapes — the core of fast array thinking.

mockTasks.q: In scikit-learn, fit() then predict() means:
choices: Fit on test, predict on train
Learn parameters from training data, then apply to new data
Both happen on the same data
mockTasks.explain: The estimator contract: fit learns from train, predict/transform applies to new data.

mockTasks.q: The KV cache in transformer inference:
choices: Caches keys and values so each new token avoids recomputing past positions
mockTasks.explain: Autoregressive decoding reuses cached K/V — the key inference optimization, at the cost of memory per token.

choices: Optimizing preferences directly without training a separate reward model + RL loop
mockTasks.explain: Direct Preference Optimization turns preference pairs into a classification-style loss — alignment without the RL machinery.

mockTasks.q: LLM-as-judge evaluation is risky because judges:
choices: Can be biased, flattered by style, and gamed
mockTasks.explain: Model judges show position/length bias and can be gamed — useful signal, but validate against human judgments.

choices: Dense vectors where semantic similarity becomes geometric closeness
mockTasks.explain: Embeddings map sentences to vectors so cosine similarity approximates meaning similarity — the basis of semantic search.

choices: Lexical matching is a strong, cheap baseline, especially for rare terms
mockTasks.explain: BM25’s term-frequency scoring still wins on exact/rare terms — hybrid search combines it with dense retrieval.

mockTasks.q: Least privilege for model-invoked tools means:
choices: Each tool gets only the permissions its job needs
mockTasks.explain: Narrow, typed tools with minimal permissions bound the blast radius when the model misuses a tool.

blocks.body: **Precision** = TP/(TP+FP) — of predicted positives, how many were right. **Recall** = TP/(TP+FN) — of actual positives, how many were found. **Calibration**: predicted 0.7 ≈ happens 70% of the time. **Leakage**: future/target info reaching training — the fake-0.99 factory.

**Bagging** averages models → cuts variance. **Boosting** fits residuals sequentially → cuts bias. **Baseline first**: simple model sets the bar. **Ablation**: remove a component, measure the drop — credit assignment.

**Attention**: weighted mix of values by query-key similarity. **LoRA**: low-rank weight updates, base frozen. **RAG**: retrieve → rerank → generate with citations. **Eval harness**: golden set + regression checks on every change.

- Split before any learned transformation
- All preprocessing inside the Pipeline / ColumnTransformer
- Fit on train only; test touched once at the end
- Datetime features use only as-of-prediction-time info
- Target encodings computed inside CV folds
- Seeds, versions, and run logs recorded
AUC ≈ 0.99 on a hard problem · test accuracy >> cross-val accuracy · a feature that ‘shouldn’t be that predictive’ · timestamps after the label date.

**Context length** → KV-cache memory and quadratic attention cost. **Batching** → throughput up, latency up. **Quantization** → smaller/faster, verify quality after. **Caching** → repeated prompts nearly free. Model the **cost per 1k requests** before promising a feature.

**Chunking** decides what retrieval can find. **Reranking** buys precision on top of recall. **Evals**: task-specific sets you own; benchmarks leak and judges flatter. **Regression suite** on every model/prompt change.

- Feature flags for model-backed behavior
- Guardrails: input validation + output controls
- UX for uncertainty: confidence, citations, corrections
- Feedback logging → turns usage into eval data
- Cost controls: budgets, caching, routing
- Rollback plan and shadow deploys
Schemas as contracts · narrow, typed tools · least privilege · handle tool errors · test tool-using paths like any integration.

answerBank.q: Walk me through how you’d take an ML model from notebook to production.
answerBank.a: Frame the problem and success metric first, then build a simple baseline with a leak-free pipeline (all preprocessing inside, fit on train only). Evaluate on a held-out set touched once, iterate with experiment discipline (seeds, versions, logs), and ship behind an API with input validation, prediction logging, and a rollback plan — shadow-deployed before full cutover.

answerBank.q: Your model scores 0.99 AUC but flops in production. What happened?
answerBank.a: Almost certainly target leakage: a feature computed with post-label information, or preprocessing fit on the full dataset before splitting. I’d audit every feature’s availability timestamp relative to prediction time, move all learned transformations inside a train-only pipeline, re-split honestly, and report the real number — then add a leakage checklist to the team’s review process.

answerBank.q: When do you choose gradient-boosted trees over deep learning on tabular data?
answerBank.a: Trees are the default for tabular data up to large-but-not-massive scale: they handle mixed types and missing values, need less tuning, train fast on CPU, and explain well via SHAP. I’d reach for deep learning when there’s unstructured signal (text/images), very high-cardinality categoricals that benefit from embeddings, or transfer learning from a pretrained model — and I’d prove the choice with a baseline comparison, not an assumption.

answerBank.q: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
answerBank.a: Two layers: retrieval quality (recall@k on a golden question-passage set, plus rerank precision) and end-to-end answer quality (faithfulness to cited passages, task success judged against human labels on a sample). I’d keep a regression suite run on every chunking/prompt/model change, track the failure catalog, and distrust vendor benchmarks — only task-specific evals I own count.

answerBank.q: Explain LoRA and when you’d use it.
answerBank.a: LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and trains small low-rank update matrices injected into the layers — a fraction of the parameters, so adaptation is cheap and the base model stays intact. I’d use it when I need task/style adaptation on a modest data budget, and I’d always evaluate before vs. after on my own task set, because fine-tuning can also make a model worse.

answerBank.q: How do you keep LLM feature costs under control?
answerBank.a: Model cost per 1k requests up front; pick the smallest model that passes the eval bar; cache repeated prompts; batch where latency allows; quantize for self-hosted serving and verify quality after; route simple queries to cheaper models. Then monitor spend per feature with budgets and alerts — cost is a design constraint, not a surprise at the invoice.

answerBank.q: A stakeholder asks for an AI solution to a vague problem. What’s your first move?
answerBank.a: A pre-mortem, not a model: is ML even the answer (honest checklist), what’s the success metric, what are the latency/cost/data/regulatory constraints, and what’s the thinnest slice that could prove value. I’d write the one-page framing doc and get agreement on the metric before touching data — most AI projects fail before the first model, on problem definition.
